facts.text: John Beaulieu, the postmaster, gave the community its name when he opened the first post office in 1891.
Before the county existed, a French‑Canadian trader of Ojibwe descent, John H. Beaulieu, set up a trading post on the Wild Rice River in 1868.
From 1884 to 1915, the Wild Rice River Boarding and Day School operated in Beaulieu, serving as an American Indian residential school.
The Wild Rice River flows west through Beaulieu, eventually joining the Red River at the North Dakota state line.
Early economic activity in Beaulieu revolved around the trading post, which served as a hub for barter with Ojibwe residents, trading furs for textiles and tools.
Today, Beaulieu remains a rural, sparsely populated area that reflects its historical roots in frontier trade and early community development amid Minnesota's northern woodlands.
